q: 1. In a bar of large length when held vertically and subjected to a load at its lower end, its own-weight, produces additional stress. The maximum stress will be
options: at every point of the bar
explain: The internal axial force (and hence stress) accumulates from the free lower end upward due to self-weight, so the maximum total stress (applied load + accumulated self-weight) occurs at the top, built-in cross-section.

q: 2. If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section of the prismatic bar, becomes
explain: For a bar of uniform section carrying its own weight and load, if stress must remain exactly at the (constant) working stress everywhere despite increasing self-weight force with length, the theoretical cross-sectional area needed tends to infinity (this describes the limiting/idealized case of a bar of uniform strength).

q: 3. The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length, is
explain: As established earlier, a conical bar's self-weight elongation is exactly one-third that of a prismatic bar of the same length.

q: 4. The Young's modulus of elasticity of steel is
explain: The standard value for steel modulus ($E$) is $200 	ext{ GPa}$ or $200 	ext{ kN/mm}^2$.

q: 5. A square column carries a load P at the centroid of one of the quarters of the square, the side of the main square, the combined bending stress will be
explain: Applying combined direct and bending stress formulas for a load placed at the centroid of one quadrant (eccentricity a/4 in both directions) of a square column of side a gives a combined stress of 3P/a².

q: 6. Creep of material is the property indicated by
options: elongation of the materials caused by changes in material properties
time dependent strain of the materials
shortening caused by shrinkage of the member
decrease in volume of the materials affected by the weather conditions
explain: Creep is specifically defined as permanent deformation under a constant load over time.

q: 7. The area of the core of a column of cross sectional area A is
explain: For standard rectangular/square columns, the core area (region of no tension) works out to A/18 of the total cross-sectional area, a known ratio derived from the middle-third rhombus geometry.

q: 8. The shear center may be defined as
options: the point through which the resultant of the shear stress pass
the point about which the moment of shear flow is zero
the centre of gravity of section
explain: The shear center is the point where a load produces only bending and no torsion.

q: 9. The ratio of the area of cross section of a circular section to the area of its core is
explain: Core radius of a circle is r/4, so core area = π(r/4)² = πr²/16; ratio of total area (πr²) to core area is 16.

q: 10. The shear center in the case of T-beam section is
options: at the C.G. of the section
at the neutral axis of the section
on the C.G. horizontal plane and away from C.G. within the leg projections
explain: For sections with one axis of symmetry, the shear center lies on that axis. In a T-beam, it is typically at the junction of the web and flange.

q: 11. When a closed coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial tensile load the material of the spring will be subjected to
explain: In a closed-coil helical spring under axial load, the wire is primarily subjected to torsional shear stress due to the load acting at an offset (radius) from the wire's axis.

q: 12. The shear flow in a section can be defined as
options: total shear stress at a point
explain: Shear flow ($q$) is the shear force per unit length along a cross-section ($q = 	au \cdot t$).

q: 13. When a close coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial twist, the material of the spring will be subjected to
explain: When a closed-coil spring is subjected to an axial twisting moment (about its own axis), the wire is subjected to bending stress (the roles of torsion and bending swap compared to axial loading).

q: 14. When a thin cylindrical shell is subjected to internal fluid pressure, which of the following stress is developed in its wall ?
explain: Internal pressure in cylinders creates both hoop (circumferential) and longitudinal stresses.

q: 15. If a shaft subjected to pure torsion cracks, the crack will start
explain: Since shear stress due to torsion is maximum at the outer surface (periphery) and zero at the centre, cracks in a shaft under torsion initiate at the periphery.

q: 16. Shear strain theory for the failure of a material at elastic limit is due to
explain: The shear strain energy (distortion energy) theory of failure is attributed to Von Mises (also known as the Von Mises-Hencky theory).

q: 17. Gradually applied static loads do not change with time their
explain: A static load, by definition, is applied gradually and remains constant in magnitude, direction, and point of application over time — hence 'all of these'.

q: 18. The sum of normal stress is
explain: The sum of normal stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes at a point (σx + σy) is a stress invariant — it remains constant regardless of the orientation of the planes chosen.

q: 19. The radius of Mohr's circle for two equal unlike principle stresses of magnitude P is
explain: For two equal but unlike (opposite sign) principal stresses +P and −P, the radius of Mohr's circle = (σ1−σ2)/2 = (P−(−P))/2 = P.

q: 20. Shear stress on principal planes is
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which shear stress is zero (only normal stress acts).

q: 21. The bending moment at a section tends to bend or deflect the beam and the internal stresses resist bending. The resistance offered by the internal stresses, to the bending, is called
explain: The internal resisting stress developed within a beam's cross-section to counter the external bending moment is termed bending stress.

q: 22. The neutral axis of the cross-section of a beam is that axis at which the bending stress is
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the axis in the cross-section where bending stress (and strain) is zero.

q: 23. When a cantilever beam is loaded at its free end, the maximum compressive stress will develop at
explain: For a cantilever loaded downward at its free end, the top fibres near the fixed support stretch (tension) while the bottom fibres compress, so maximum compressive stress develops at the bottom fibre.

q: 24. A beam of uniform strength may be obtained by
options: keeping the width uniform and varying the depth
keeping the depth uniform and varying the width
varying the width and depth both
explain: A beam of uniform strength can be achieved by varying depth alone, width alone, or both together, as long as the section modulus varies appropriately with the moment — hence any of these approaches works.

q: 25. At the neutral axis of a beam
options: the layers are subjected to maximum bending stress
the layers are subjected to minimum bending stress
the layers are subjected to compression
the layers do not undergo any strain
explain: Fibres along the neutral axis experience zero strain (neither elongation nor compression) during bending, by definition of the neutral axis.

q: 26. The neutral axis of a beam is subjected to ............. stress.
explain: Since strain at the neutral axis is zero, and stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law), the bending stress there is also zero.

q: 27. The neutral axis of a transverse section of a beam passes through the centre of gravity of the section and is
options: in the same plane in which the beam bends
at right angle to the plane in which the beam bends
explain: The neutral axis lies perpendicular to the plane of bending (the plane containing the applied loads and curvature), while passing through the section's centroid.

q: 28. In a beam subjected to pure bending, the intensity of stress in any fibre is ............. the distance of the fibre from the neutral axis.
explain: From the flexure formula σ = My/I, bending stress varies linearly (directly proportional) with distance y from the neutral axis.

q: 29. A the neutral axis of a beam, the shear stress is
explain: For most common sections (rectangular, circular), the shear stress distribution is parabolic and peaks at the neutral axis (where it is maximum), not zero.

q: 30. The ratio of maximum shear stress developed in a rectangular beam and a circular beam of the same cross-sectional area is
explain: Comparing the maximum shear stress factors of a rectangle (1.5×average) and circle (1.333×average) of equal area, working through the equal-area condition gives a ratio of 9/8.

q: 31. A beam of triangular section is placed with its base horizontal. The maximum shear stress occurs at
options: centre of gravity of the triangle
explain: For a triangular section with base horizontal, detailed analysis shows the maximum shear stress occurs at mid-height, not exactly at the centroid or base.

q: 32. Coefficient of wind resistance of a circular surface is
explain: The standard coefficient of wind resistance (pressure coefficient) for a circular (cylindrical) surface, as used in practical wind load calculations, is taken as 2/3.

q: 33. The ratio of circumferential stress to the longitudinal stress in the walls of a cylindrical shell due to flowing liquid is
explain: For a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure, circumferential (hoop) stress = pd/2t while longitudinal stress = pd/4t, giving a ratio of 2:1.

q: 34. Shear center of a half circular section of radius r and a constant thickness, lies at a distance of from the center where x is
explain: For a thin semicircular section, the shear centre lies at a distance of 4r/π from the centre of the circle, a standard derived result.

q: 35. Euler's formula holds good only for
explain: Euler's buckling formula is derived assuming purely elastic instability and is valid only for long, slender columns (high slenderness ratio).

q: 36. The Rankine's formula holds good for
explain: Rankine's empirical formula was developed specifically to bridge the gap between crushing (short column) and buckling (long column) failure, making it applicable across both ranges.

q: 37. In case of eccentrically loaded struts ............. is preferred
explain: For eccentrically loaded struts, a composite section is preferred as it can be tailored (e.g., unsymmetric distribution) to better resist the resulting combined bending and axial stresses.

q: 38. In a tensile test, when the material is stressed beyond beyond elastic limit, the tensile strain ............. as compared to the stress.
explain: Beyond the elastic limit, the stress-strain curve flattens considerably, meaning strain increases much more rapidly than the corresponding increase in stress.

q: 39. The stress at which the extension of the material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: This describes the yield point, where strain increases disproportionately compared to the increase in load/stress.

q: 40. The stress developed in the material without any permanent set is called
explain: The elastic limit is defined as the maximum stress up to which the material returns to its original shape completely (no permanent set) after unloading.

q: 41. The tensile test is carried on ............. materials.
explain: Tensile tests (measuring elongation, necking, ductile yielding behavior) are primarily meaningful and carried out on ductile materials.

q: 42. The compression test is carried on ............. materials.
explain: Compression tests are the standard test method for brittle materials (like cast iron, concrete), which are weak in tension but strong in compression.

q: 43. Factor of safety is defined as the ratio of
explain: Factor of safety is standardly defined as the ratio of the ultimate (or yield) stress to the permissible working stress used in design.

q: 44. The ratio of lateral strain to axial strain of a homogenous material is known as
explain: By definition, Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to axial (longitudinal) strain.

q: 45. The normal and tangential components of stress on an inclined plane through to the direction of the force will be equal to
explain: For a uniaxial stress acting on an inclined plane, the normal and tangential (shear) stress components become equal when the plane is inclined at 45° to the force direction.

q: 46. The locus of the end point of the resultant of the normal and tangential components of the stress on an inclined plane is
explain: As the inclination of the plane varies, the resultant stress vector's endpoint traces out an ellipse (the stress ellipse), similar to the momental ellipse for inertia.

q: 47. Principal planes are subjected to
options: normal stresses as well as tangential stresses
explain: By definition, a principal plane carries only normal stress with zero shear (tangential) stress.

q: 48. The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on the configuration
explain: While maximum shear stress is at the neutral axis for symmetric sections like rectangles and circles, for unsymmetrical sections (like T-sections) it can occur elsewhere, so it depends on the section's configuration.

q: 49. In an I section almost all the shear force is taken by
options: half the depth of each flange
explain: In an I-section, due to its geometry, the thin web carries the vast majority (typically over 90%) of the total shear force, while the flanges carry very little.

q: 50. Twisting moment is a moment applied in the plane of cross-section acting about
explain: Twisting (torsional) moment acts about the longitudinal axis of the member, causing rotation of cross-sections relative to each other.
